samples.generated: In the days of my youth, I found myself drawn to the new high-rise building near the river that had recently been completed in our neighborhood. It was a tall, sleek structure that seemed to pierce the sky, and its empty halls and rooms seemed to call to me. I spent many hours in that building, and I can remember it all too clearly. When I walked in one day, I found myself standing in a long, dark corridor, the light from the door flickering and dancing across the walls. I looked around and saw that the buildings were all empty, but I could imagine that they were full. The long, high doors seemed to lead to other rooms. I walked to the third floor, and there I saw a long room with a desk in the center of it. On the desk was a lot of paper and a pen. I sat down and started writing.

samples.prompt: Write a personal essay that revisits a place from your past, comparing how it appears now with your memories of it from years ago.
samples.generated:
I had the pleasure of visiting the town of Montparnasse in Paris a little more than ten years ago, and it was a little more than twenty years before that. As I walked through the streets and squares I had known so well in my youth, I felt the same sense of joy and excitement that I had experienced on my first visits. At that time there were no taxis; I had to go to the bottom of the hill and walk to the top; I had to go up and down in the street; I had to go round the back of the café; I had to be careful of the tram rails; I had to be careful of the horses; I had to walk with my eyes open all the time, for the streets were not well lit. In the spring and autumn, I had to be careful not to get wet, for the puddles were deep and the rain was heavy.

In the winter I had to walk in the rain, in the snow, in the slush; and I had to be careful of the ice, for the pavement was rough and slippery; I had to be careful of the horses, for they were dirty and untamable.

We have read of some celebrated philosopher who was so absent-minded
that he paid a call at his own house. My own absent-mindedness is
extreme, and my philosophy, of course, is the marvel of men and angels.
But I never quite managed to be so absent-minded as that. Some yards at
least from my own door, something vaguely familiar has always caught
my eye; and thus the joke has been spoiled. Of course I have quite
constantly walked into another man's house, thinking it was my own
house; my visits became almost monotonous. But walking into my own house
and thinking it was another man's house is a flight of poetic detachment
still beyond me. Something of the sensations that such an absent-minded
man must feel I really felt the other day; and very pleasant sensations
they were. The best parts of every proper romance are the first chapter
and the last chapter; and to knock at a strange door and find a nice
wife would be to concentrate the beginning and end of all romance.
